def Target : Prop :=
  ∀ (Fm S₀ S : Type) [LogicalConnective Fm] [LogicalNeutral Fm] [Entailment S₀ Fm] [Entailment S Fm]
    (𝓑 : S₀) (𝓢 : S) [Entailment.Cl 𝓑] [Entailment.Cl 𝓢] (K F : Fm → Fm),
    Def1 𝓑 K → 𝓑 ⪯ 𝓢 → Def2 𝓢 K → Def4 𝓢 K →
    𝓑 ⊢ F (∼F ⊥) 🡒 F ⊥ →
    (∀ φ, 𝓢 ⊢ K (K φ 🡒 F φ)) →
    𝓢 ⊢ K (∼K (∼F ⊥))
a_raw: {"translation":"Target is defined to be the following proposition. For every choice of types Fm, S₀ and S, of sentence connectives and truth and falsehood constants on Fm, and of provability relations for S₀ and S on Fm, take any systems 𝓑 : S₀ and 𝓢 : S. Assume that each system proves every classical propositional tautology and is closed under modus ponens. Then for every pair of functions K, F : Fm → Fm, the following hypotheses, in order, imply the conclusion: (1) for every sentence φ, if 𝓑 proves φ then 𝓑 proves K(φ); (2) every sentence provable in 𝓑 is provable in 𝓢; (3) for every sentence φ and then every sentence ψ, 𝓢 proves K(φ 🡒 ψ) 🡒 (K(φ) 🡒 K(ψ)); (4) for every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K(K(φ) 🡒 φ); (5) 𝓑 proves the single implication F(∼(F(⊥))) 🡒 F(⊥); and (6) for every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K(K(φ) 🡒 F(φ)). The conclusion is that 𝓢 proves K(∼(K(∼(F(⊥))))). Here 🡒 and ∼ are connectives inside the sentences. Neither system is assumed consistent. The closure rule in (1) is required of 𝓑, not of 𝓢; (4) does not require 𝓢 to prove the unwrapped implication K(φ) 🡒 φ, and no fixed-point hypothesis on F is required."}
translation: Target is defined to be the following proposition. For every choice of types Fm, S₀ and S, of sentence connectives and truth and falsehood constants on Fm, and of provability relations for S₀ and S on Fm, take any systems 𝓑 : S₀ and 𝓢 : S. Assume that each system proves every classical propositional tautology and is closed under modus ponens. Then for every pair of functions K, F : Fm → Fm, the following hypotheses, in order, imply the conclusion: (1) for every sentence φ, if 𝓑 proves φ then 𝓑 proves K(φ); (2) every sentence provable in 𝓑 is provable in 𝓢; (3) for every sentence φ and then every sentence ψ, 𝓢 proves K(φ 🡒 ψ) 🡒 (K(φ) 🡒 K(ψ)); (4) for every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K(K(φ) 🡒 φ); (5) 𝓑 proves the single implication F(∼(F(⊥))) 🡒 F(⊥); and (6) for every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K(K(φ) 🡒 F(φ)). The conclusion is that 𝓢 proves K(∼(K(∼(F(⊥))))). Here 🡒 and ∼ are connectives inside the sentences. Neither system is assumed consistent. The closure rule in (1) is required of 𝓑, not of 𝓢; (4) does not require 𝓢 to prove the unwrapped implication K(φ) 🡒 φ, and no fixed-point hypothesis on F is required.

divergences.description: Lean replaces the concrete assumption that S includes EA with inclusion of provable sentences between abstract classical systems. It assumes selected epistemic properties explicitly: necessitation for the base, and distribution and known factivity in S. It does not require the base to have the full axioms or language of EA.

The arbitrary sentence functions K and F need not arise from the syntax of L_EA. In particular, Lean does not require F φ to be obtained from a single one-free-variable formula by substituting the numeral for the Gödel number of φ; it models neither that coding nor object-language quantification.

judgement.summary: Apart from the declared proviso, the pointwise hypothesis and conclusion match Theorem 4, including the scope of provability and the nesting of K, on the reading Con(F) = ¬F(⊥). The proviso restricts the result to F for which the base proves F(Con(F)) → F(⊥), so this is not the unrestricted printed theorem.
